records.sourceFile: Cluster vs traditional training programs - Changes in the force velocity relationship.pdf

paper.citation: Rial-Vázquez J, Mayo X, Tufano JJ, Fariñas J, Rúa-Alonso M, Iglesias-Soler E. Cluster vs. traditional training programmes: changes in the force-velocity relationship. Sports Biomech. 2022;21(1):85-103.
paper.abstract: A 5-week randomised trial compared traditional and cluster set structures, matched for load, volume and rest, on the force-velocity (F-V) profile of bench press and squat. Cluster training shifted the squat F-V profile toward velocity, while the two set structures changed the bench press profile in similar ways.
paper.tldr: With load, volume and rest matched, cluster sets moved the squat force-velocity profile toward higher velocity and kept velocity loss lower than traditional sets. Bench press profiles changed similarly under both set structures, so the benefit may be specific to lower-body work.
paper.methods: Participants were randomised to traditional (4 x 8 reps, 5 min rest), cluster (16 x 2 reps, 1 min intra-set rest) or control groups, all at 10RM load for 10 sessions over 5 weeks. F-V profiles were derived from a linear velocity transducer during a progressive 1RM test before and after training, and velocity loss, lactate and accumulated work were tracked across sessions. Group x time ANOVAs were used for the outcome measures.
paper.findings: In the squat, cluster training produced a less steep slope, a higher velocity intercept (V0) and a higher F1RM/F0 ratio, while traditional training raised only the force intercept (F0); squat mean propulsive power at the best load rose only after cluster training. Bench press F0, V0 and Pmax rose in both training groups with no change in slope. 1RM rose in both training groups but not in control, and cluster sets produced lower peak lactate, less within-session velocity loss and a higher average training velocity in the squat (P = 0.049).
paper.limitations: Small sample of mixed-sex students with about 3 months of resistance training experience, and a 5-week, 10-session intervention. Table 1 reports a significant time x group 1RM interaction for bench press (P = 0.001) and squat (P < 0.001), but the paper reports no traditional vs cluster 1RM contrast, so the Discussion's 'similar gains' is untested. Smith machine load limits (21.4 kg minimum) restricted data at high velocities, especially for women, and 4.52% of F-V fits had R-squared below 0.800.
paper.practicalImplications: For squat work aimed at velocity, cluster sets at 10RM (2 reps with 1 minute intra-set rest) kept velocity higher across a session than 4 x 8 with 5 minutes of rest, with equal total rest. Both set structures raised 1RM over 5 weeks, and the authors describe the gains as similar, so set structure can be chosen around the velocity or force emphasis wanted. These results come from students with limited lifting experience and should not be assumed for advanced athletes.
paper.athleteDev: Cluster sets may help a squat program shift the force-velocity profile toward velocity with less velocity loss per session. Bench press changes did not differ between set structures, so set configuration may matter more for lower-body than upper-body work. The findings come from 5 weeks of training in students, not from athletes in a competitive season.
paper.rtp: Not a return-to-sport study. Participants were injury-free, and no injury or rehabilitation outcome was measured, so the paper does not support cluster sets as a rehabilitation or return-to-sport loading strategy.

records.sourceFile: Coaches and players perceptions of    training dose - Not a perfect match.pdf

paper.citation: Brink MS, Frencken WGP, Jordet G, Lemmink KAPM. Coaches' and Players' Perceptions of Training Dose: Not a Perfect Match. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2014;9:497-502.
paper.abstract: Across a full competitive season, session RPE and duration reported by 33 elite youth soccer players were compared with the intensity and duration coaches had planned for each session. Players rated training as harder than intended, and the coach-player correlations were weak.
paper.tldr: Young elite soccer players rated their sessions as harder than coaches intended, and their ratings agreed only weakly with the coach's plan over a whole season. Planned easy and intermediate sessions felt harder to players, while planned hard sessions felt easier.
paper.methods: Before each session, coaches recorded intended exertion (session RIE, 6 to 20 scale) and planned duration for every player. About 30 minutes after each session, players rated session RPE and duration, and load was calculated as RPE x duration. Sessions were grouped as easy, intermediate or hard by intended exertion and compared using two-way ANOVA with Pearson correlations.
paper.findings: Players rated intensity (14.0 vs 13.6) and training load (944 vs 923 AU) higher than coaches intended (P < .0001), with no duration difference, and the coach-player correlations were weak (r = .24 to .49). For sessions coaches intended as easy, players rated intensity (13.3 vs 11.3) and load (884 vs 743 AU) higher, and intermediate sessions followed the same pattern, while intended hard sessions were rated lower for intensity (14.4 vs 15.3), duration and load (1004 vs 1091 AU). First-year U-17 players rated intensity higher than the coach intended (13.7 vs 13.3), and second-year players did not differ.
paper.limitations: Observational design with no injury, illness or performance outcomes, so the stated risk of overtraining and injury is not tested here. Players' accuracy with session RPE may vary, and the authors note that individual validity of RPE in young players ranges widely. Two squads with one coach each limit generalisation to other settings.
paper.practicalImplications: Compare the coach's intended exertion with each player's session RPE across the week, so that a mismatch on an easy or hard day is spotted early. The authors suggest heart rate feedback can help young players calibrate their RPE, and that players should be taught why easy days should not feel hard. Check training dose at age-group transitions, since first-year U-17 players rated their sessions harder than intended.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the gap between planned and felt sessions is a check on whether hard days are hard enough and easy days stay easy. The authors argue that players who train harder than planned on easy days may not recover and adapt, so comparing planned and felt load is a practical way to spot that pattern.
paper.rtp: Not a return-to-sport paper. It studies training dose perception in academy players and measured no injury, recovery or clearance outcome, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Comparison of EMG activity during hip extension exercises under gravitational or inertial loading conditions.pdf

paper.citation: Martín-San Agustín R, Castillo-Ballesta L, Llobat Sancho J, Esbri-Navarro R, Sánchez-Barbadora M. Comparison of Electromyographic Activity During Hip Extension Exercises Under Gravitational or Inertial Loading Conditions. Sports Health. 2021.
paper.abstract: Electromyography study of 15 resistance-trained men performing unilateral straight knee bridge, 45-degree hip extension and stiff-leg deadlift under gravitational and inertial loading, with biceps femoris, semitendinosus, gluteus maximus and gracilis recorded. Inertial loading produced greater concentric hamstring activation, and the knee bridge and hip extension produced greater biceps femoris and semitendinosus activation than the stiff-leg deadlift.
paper.tldr: In 15 resistance-trained men, inertial loading produced higher concentric hamstring and gluteus maximus activation than gravitational loading, and the knee bridge and hip extension produced more biceps femoris activity than the stiff-leg deadlift. This is a single-session EMG study in healthy men, so it describes activation patterns rather than injury or strength outcomes.
paper.methods: Within-subject, repeated-measures EMG study (the paper's header labels it cross-sectional) in which each participant completed three sessions a week apart: familiarization, determination of the load giving maximum concentric power with a linear encoder, and EMG recording at that load in randomized, counterbalanced order. Surface EMG from the biceps femoris, semitendinosus, gluteus maximus and gracilis was normalized to MVIC, averaged over five repetitions, and analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.
paper.findings: In the concentric phase, inertial loading exceeded gravitational loading for biceps femoris (15%, P = 0.003), semitendinosus (9.9%, P = 0.007) and gluteus maximus (21.5%, P = 0.001). In the eccentric phase, only gluteus maximus differed between loading types (18.1% higher with inertial loading, P = 0.003), and a modality by exercise interaction showed this for the knee bridge and stiff-leg deadlift. Knee bridge and hip extension produced higher biceps femoris activity than stiff-leg deadlift in both phases, and the biceps femoris to semitendinosus ratio was higher for hip extension than stiff-leg deadlift in both phases (concentric 1.50 vs 1.24, P = 0.002; eccentric 1.41 vs 1.05, P = 0.001).
paper.limitations: The study included only 15 healthy men with no recent injury, so the patterns may not apply to women or to athletes with a strain history, and only three exercises were tested. Concentric power was used to set the load, which may influence the eccentric comparison. The abstract attributes the eccentric semitendinosus difference to hip extension, but the Results and Table 2 attribute it to the knee bridge (P = 0.008), the Results report the eccentric ratio for inertial stiff-leg deadlift as a percentage (1.17% vs 0.93), and the conclusion's claim of high biceps femoris specificity for the knee bridge is not supported by a significant ratio difference.
paper.practicalImplications: When hamstring work is programmed, this study suggests that the knee bridge and 45-degree hip extension produce more hamstring activation than the stiff-leg deadlift, and that hip extension is more biceps femoris selective than the stiff-leg deadlift. The concentric advantage of inertial loading does not extend to the eccentric hamstring phase in this study, so the paper does not show that inertial loading is superior for eccentric hamstring work.
paper.athleteDev: The study measures muscle activation, not strength or power gains. Inertial loading produced higher concentric hamstring and gluteal activation, which the authors use as a rationale for inertial hip-extension exercise, but no training outcome was measured.
paper.rtp: All participants were healthy and injury-free, so the study does not show which exercises are safe or effective for athletes returning from hamstring strain. The authors suggest hip extension may suit biceps femoris-related rehabilitation, but the paper does not test rehabilitation or re-injury outcomes, so that suggestion rests only on activation ratios.

records.sourceFile: Comparison of the Effects of Velocity-Based Training Methods and Traditional 1RM-Percent-Based Training Prescription on Acute Kinetic and Kinematic Variables.pdf

paper.citation: Banyard HG, Tufano JJ, Delgado J, Thompson SW, Nosaka K. Comparison of the Effects of Velocity-Based Training Methods and Traditional 1RM-Percent-Based Training Prescription on Acute Kinetic and Kinematic Variables. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019; ahead of print.
paper.abstract: Fifteen resistance-trained men completed four randomized back squat sessions at 80% 1RM: percent-based training, a load-velocity profile session, and two velocity-loss-threshold sessions (fixed sets and variable sets, each with a 20% velocity loss threshold). Load-velocity and fixed-set sessions produced faster mean and peak velocities than percent-based training, and both involved less time under tension. Force, power and total work were similar across sessions.
paper.tldr: In a single session of back squats at 80% 1RM, two velocity-based methods (load adjusted to a velocity target, and fixed sets stopped at a 20% velocity loss) let trained men move the bar faster with less time under tension, while force and power stayed similar. These are acute results and do not show which method builds more strength.
paper.methods: Randomized crossover design in 15 resistance-trained men who completed four sessions 96 h apart: 5 x 5 at 80% 1RM (PBT); 5 x 5 with the load changed by 5% 1RM between sets whenever set mean velocity was more than 0.06 m/s away from the target taken from each person's load-velocity profile (LVP); 5 sets at 80% 1RM ended at a 20% velocity loss (FSVL20); and 25 total repetitions at 80% 1RM split into as many sets as needed to stay within a 20% velocity loss (VSVL20). Velocity was measured with four linear position transducers and force and power with a force plate during the concentric phase.
paper.findings: Mean velocity was 0.60 m/s in LVP and 0.58 m/s in FSVL20 versus 0.53 m/s in PBT (effect sizes 1.05 and 0.81), and peak velocity was also faster in both (effect sizes 1.12 and 0.98). LVP used a mean load of 120.5 kg versus 122.4 kg for PBT (not significantly different), mean repetition time under tension (total and concentric) was lower in LVP, and session totals were lower in FSVL20, but not in VSVL20. FSVL20 completed 23.6 repetitions versus 25 in the other sessions, and VSVL20 took 9:02 versus 10:36 min for PBT with no significant difference in velocity, force, power, work or load.
paper.limitations: Only 15 men were tested in one acute session, and chronic outcomes were not measured. Participants were told to stop sets or had loads changed when velocity targets were missed, so they could tell whether their previous set was above or below threshold, and two VSVL20 participants needed six sets. The velocity-loss threshold was set from the single warm-up repetition at 80% 1RM.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches with velocity-monitoring equipment can use a velocity target or a 20% velocity loss threshold to limit repetitions and keep bar speed higher within a session. The study does not show that this improves strength or power over a season, so the choice should follow the training goal.
paper.athleteDev: For a strength-focused block in healthy, resistance-trained men, the LVP and fixed-set sets kept bar speed higher and reduced time under tension compared with percent-based sets, with similar force and power output. Whether this leads to more strength or power over weeks is not shown here.
paper.rtp: This study tested healthy men without musculoskeletal injury and cannot inform return to sport. It should not be used to set rehabilitation loads or to judge the safety of velocity-based training after injury.

records.sourceFile: Connective Adaptive Resistance Exercise (CARE) Machines for Accentuated Eccentric and Eccentric-Only Exercise - Introduction to an Emerging Conc.pdf

paper.citation: Nuzzo JL, Pinto MD, Nosaka K. Connective Adaptive Resistance Exercise (CARE) Machines for Accentuated Eccentric and Eccentric-Only Exercise: Introduction to an Emerging Concept. Sports Medicine. 2023.
paper.abstract: This concept paper introduces connected adaptive resistance exercise (CARE) machines, which adjust load in real time to allow accentuated eccentric and eccentric-only training. The authors review existing eccentric equipment and present preliminary machine data from laboratory and non-laboratory use.
paper.tldr: CARE machines adjust resistance within and between repetitions, which lets users perform eccentric overload and eccentric-only sets without spotters or releasers. The authors present the concept and preliminary load data, but the paper does not show effects on strength, muscle size, injury or rehabilitation.
paper.methods: Narrative review of resistance equipment and practitioner survey data, with a description of one CARE machine (Vitruvian Trainer+). Preliminary data came from one individual performing one 25-repetition maximal biceps curl set in each of two modes in the laboratory, and from machine-recorded loads of a random sample of 100 male users (2,124 accentuated sets) and 26 of those men (135 eccentric-only sets) in non-laboratory settings.
paper.findings: In the non-laboratory sample, average eccentric loads exceeded concentric loads (eccentric:concentric ratio 1.42 across 18,174 accentuated repetitions; 4.99 across 900 eccentric-only repetitions from 26 men), with sets done at varied, unrecorded intensities. In the single-person laboratory example, the machine's delivered load fell 61.4% (eccentric) and 85.5% (concentric) from repetition 2 to 24 in the accentuated set, and 37.9% (eccentric) in the eccentric-only set. The authors also cite two earlier experiments reporting strong correlations (r >= 0.94) between machine concentric strength and a dumbbell 1RM test.
paper.limitations: The paper is a concept piece with uncontrolled, machine-generated load data and no outcome measures; the laboratory data come from one individual and the field data from machine users of unstated training status. Reliability, validity and effectiveness of CARE machines are described as limited, and two authors previously worked for the company that makes the machine described. The authors' statement that home machines 'appear to provide a stimulus sufficient for neuromuscular adaptation' rests on load data only, and they note longer-term training studies are required.
paper.practicalImplications: Where eccentric overload or eccentric-only work is planned but spotters or releasers are not available, a CARE machine may be a practical option to evaluate. Its load outputs do not show training benefit, so any program change should be assessed against local outcome measures. Practitioners should weigh the company link when reading the machine's validation data.
paper.athleteDev: CARE machines may allow eccentric overload, eccentric-only sets and automatic drop sets without spotters or releasers, which could widen the options for strength programs. The paper does not show that these methods improve strength, power or sport performance.
paper.rtp: This paper cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It mentions rehabilitation as a possible use, but it reports no clinical outcomes, injury data or rehabilitation trials.

records.sourceFile: Core stability in athletes - A critical analysis of      current guidelines.pdf

paper.citation: Wirth K, Hartmann H, Mickel C, Szilvas E, Keiner M, Sander A. Core Stability in Athletes: A Critical Analysis of Current Guidelines. Sports Med. 2016.
paper.abstract: Core stability exercise guidelines for athletes were adapted from back pain rehabilitation, and most exercise specifications have not been tested for effectiveness or compared with strength-training loads. The authors critically analyze concepts including the global and local muscle classification, selective activation, trunk-rotation exercises and training on unstable surfaces. They recommend classical strength-training exercises because these provide the stimuli needed for adaptation.
paper.tldr: Core stability guidelines borrowed from back pain rehabilitation have little evidence in athletes. The authors recommend classical strength training over selective core exercises and unstable-surface training.
paper.methods: Narrative critical analysis of the literature on core stability, trunk muscle EMG, and unstable-surface training. No systematic search strategy is described. The authors examine back pain guidelines, EMG studies of transversus abdominis and multifidus activation, and studies comparing stable and unstable squat training.
paper.findings: The authors state that the corset-like, feed-forward stabilizing role claimed for transversus abdominis rests on unilateral EMG recordings and that selective activation deficits or selective atrophy of deep trunk muscles have not been shown. They report that loads in unstable conditions are about 40 percent lower than in stable conditions, citing McBride et al. and Saeterbakken and Fimland, and that no longitudinal study has shown superiority of unstable-surface training. Citing Lederman and others, they conclude that the global and local muscle classification is inappropriate because trunk muscles act together in task-specific patterns.
paper.limitations: The conclusions depend heavily on the absence of evidence, and the authors do not describe a search, so the literature they critique cannot be reproduced. The authors note the limits of surface EMG, including crosstalk, subcutaneous fat and normalization to MVC.
paper.practicalImplications: Exercises labelled core stability, functional or specific should not be assumed to strengthen deep trunk muscles or to outperform conventional strength training. Programs for athletes can prioritize loaded classical strength exercises, and unstable-surface training should be treated as unproven. Selective activation drills should not be justified by an assumed deficit in deep trunk muscles, since the authors found no evidence of one in strength-trained athletes.
paper.athleteDev: For athletes, the paper supports building trunk strength through loaded classical exercises rather than unstable-surface or selective core drills, which the authors say lack evidence of superiority. The authors also question trunk-rotation exercises because of the shear forces they place on intervertebral discs.
paper.rtp: The paper cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It does not study injured athletes or return-to-play criteria, and its discussion of back pain concerns rehabilitation guidelines that the authors judge unsuitable for athletes.

records.sourceFile: Debunking the myths about training load injury and performance - Empirical evidence hot topics and recommendations for practitioners.pdf

paper.citation: Gabbett TJ. Debunking the myths about training load, injury and performance: empirical evidence, hot topics and recommendations for practitioners. Br J Sports Med 2018;0:1-9.
paper.abstract: This education review addresses five common myths about training load, injury and performance: that load explains all injuries, that a 10% weekly limit is a rule, that spikes and troughs must be avoided, that an acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) of 1.5 is a threshold, and that the ratio is all that matters. It draws on recent team sport and athlete studies and argues that load should be judged against chronic load and individual moderators such as age, fitness and injury history.
paper.tldr: Training load matters for injury, but no single rule, such as a 10% weekly limit or an ACWR of 1.5, explains injury risk on its own. Judge each change in load against the athlete's chronic load and individual risk factors.
paper.methods: A narrative education review by a single author, organised around five myths and drawing on recent team sport and athlete studies. No systematic search or appraisal method is described; the PubMed count in Figure 1 shows publication growth only.
paper.findings: Across 38 studies in 11 sports over five years, rapid increases in workload were associated with greater injury risk (as the author reports). In team sport, weekly load increases of 15% or more were linked to about 21% injury likelihood, against 7.5% at 10% or less, and in cricket fast bowlers, players with greater chronic workloads had a fivefold lower injury risk than those with low chronic workloads.
paper.limitations: This single-author narrative has no described search or appraisal, so the evidence chosen cannot be verified, and the author declares consulting work for high-performance organisations. Injury prediction using training load data was only slightly better than chance (AUC 0.64 to 0.76), as the review reports, and most cited work is observational in single teams of senior elite athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Judge each week's load change against the athlete's chronic load rather than a fixed 10% rule: the author's model suggests smaller increases when chronic load is extremely low or extremely high, and that larger increases may be tolerated with moderate to high chronic load and may be needed to speed rehabilitation. Avoid large week-to-week spikes but do not assume troughs are safe, since undertraining can also raise risk. Read load data alongside fitness, injury history, age and well-being rather than the ACWR alone.
paper.athleteDev: The review treats training load as a driver of both performance and injury, with higher chronic load linked to better performance and lower injury risk when built gradually. It notes that athletes who cut load most during a taper tended to improve most and that a 13-day shock block improved soccer players' performance, though most such studies in elite athletes lacked a control group.
paper.rtp: The review covers return from injury: early staged loading can shorten time to return to play, and in one study starting rehabilitation 2 days after injury rather than 9 days shortened return by 3 weeks. It also notes that building high chronic workloads may delay return to play, but it does not set return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Defining worst-case -scenario thresholds in soccer - Intensity vs volume.pdf

paper.citation: Mandorino M, Lacome M. Defining Worst-Case-Scenario Thresholds in Soccer: Intensity Versus Volume. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2024 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: This brief report describes worst-case scenario (WCS) values and the time spent above 80% and 90% of WCS for total distance (TD) and high-speed running (HSR) in professional soccer matches. Data from 31 players were compared by playing level (first team vs U19) and position. The U19 team had higher HSR WCS, and the first team spent more time above 80% and 90% of TD WCS.
paper.tldr: Peak match demands (WCS) do not show the whole picture. Time spent above 80% and 90% of WCS adds information about how often players work near their peak, and it varies by level and position.
paper.methods: Ten-hertz microtechnology (WIMU PRO) recorded 31 players across full matches in the 2022-23 season. WCS was the maximum 1-minute rolling average of TD and HSR, and time above 80% and 90% of the mean WCS was computed. Linear mixed models with player as a random effect compared level and position.
paper.findings: U19 players had higher HSR WCS than the first team (63.6 vs 56.3 m/min, P < .01, ES 0.88), and TD WCS did not differ by level. The first team spent more time above 80% (6.4 vs 5.6 min, P < .05, ES 0.27) and 90% (1.5 vs 1.2 min, P < .01, ES 0.29) of TD WCS. Midfielders had the highest TD WCS (about 208 m/min) and spent more time above 80% of TD WCS, forwards had the highest HSR WCS (about 71 m/min) and spent more time above 80% of HSR WCS, and no position differences were found above 90% of TD WCS.
paper.limitations: Single club and season, with unequal groups (18 first team, 13 U19), position groups of 6 to 10 players, and only full-match appearances included. Only a 1-minute window was tested, and the study has no measures of internal load or fatigue, so the authors' suggestion that more time near WCS probably means higher internal load is untested. Sex is not stated in the text.
paper.practicalImplications: When prescribing training for different playing roles, consider the volume of work close to WCS (time above 80% and 90%) as well as the peak WCS value. Staff can use this to compare how often first-team and U19 players work near their peak demands.
paper.athleteDev: Use time above 80% and 90% of WCS, alongside peak WCS, to compare how much work players do near their peak match demands by level and position. Training prescriptions can then match playing roles.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. This study describes match demands in squad players and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play. It cannot be used to set return-to-play loads.

records.sourceFile: Determining the optimal blood flow restriction protocol for maximizing muscle hypertrophy and strength, pressure and cuff width - A mini-review.pdf

paper.citation: Næss TC. Determining the optimal blood flow restriction protocol for maximising muscle hypertrophy and strength, pressure and cuff width: A mini-review. Journal of Human Sport & Exercise. 2021;16(4):752-759.
paper.abstract: This mini-review summarises research on blood flow restriction (BFR) training protocols, focusing on limb occlusion pressure and cuff width. It finds no uniform protocol that maximises hypertrophy and strength across studies. The author argues that occlusion pressure is best set relative to arterial occlusion pressure, and that cuff width's effect on long-term adaptation is unclear.
paper.tldr: BFR training produces gains across many protocols, but this review finds no single optimal occlusion pressure or cuff width. Setting pressure as a percentage of arterial occlusion pressure gives a more controlled stimulus, and the long-term effect of cuff width is still uncertain.
paper.methods: Mini-review of the BFR literature. The author searched PubMed, Google Scholar and Web of Science for BFR and Kaatsu terms up to June 2019, limited to English-language human studies, and checked reference lists. Protocol details (cuff width, pressure, load and volume) are tabulated for 26 study entries.
paper.findings: Absolute pressures across studies ranged from 40 to 200 mmHg, and relative pressures from 40 to 90% of arterial occlusion pressure. In Lixandrao et al. (2015), 80% vs 40% of occlusion pressure at 20% of 1RM gave a 2.44% larger muscle mass, with no meaningful difference at 40% of 1RM. Counts et al. (2016) found no significant difference in hypertrophy or strength between 40% and 90% of occlusion pressure. Narrow cuffs needed more absolute pressure to occlude flow (Jessee et al., 2016; Loenneke et al., 2012). At equal relative pressure, 100 mm and 120 mm cuffs gave similar blood flow (Mouser et al., 2018). Laurentino et al. (2016) found similar strength and size gains with 50 mm and 100 mm cuffs at 80% of occlusion pressure.
paper.limitations: Narrative mini-review with no formal quality appraisal or pooled analysis. Searches were limited to English-language articles up to June 2019. Protocols differ widely, and several Table 1 entries list cuff width as unknown, which hampers direct comparison. Evidence on cuff width and long-term adaptation is described as sparse.
paper.practicalImplications: Report occlusion pressure and cuff width in full, since these vary widely across studies and change the stimulus. Where possible, set pressure as a percentage of arterial occlusion pressure, which the author describes as more controlled than a fixed mmHg value. The author advises a lower relative pressure as the more conservative choice, and notes that higher pressures showed benefit mainly with low loads (about 20% of 1RM).
paper.athleteDev: Blood flow restriction training can add to low-load strength and size work, but the review does not identify one best pressure or cuff width. Use a relative pressure setting, record the cuff width used, and keep the protocol consistent so that changes can be read.
paper.rtp: The review mentions BFR use in rehabilitation, citing single studies on Achilles tendon rupture and extremity injury, but gives no return-to-sport protocol, criteria or injury outcomes. It cannot be used to set BFR loads or to clear an athlete to return after injury.

records.sourceFile: Different interset rest intervals during the Nordic hamstrings exercise in young male athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Drury B, Peacock D, Moran J, Cone C, Ramirez Campillo R. Different Interset Rest Intervals During the Nordic Hamstrings Exercise in Young Male Athletes. J Athl Train. 2021;56(9):952-959.
paper.abstract: This crossover study compared 1-minute and 3-minute interset rest intervals during the Nordic hamstring exercise in 10 well-trained young male team-sport athletes. Force indices and interlimb asymmetry did not differ between rest conditions or sets. Peak force declined within sets from about the fourth repetition.
paper.tldr: A 1-minute rest between Nordic hamstring sets kept force and asymmetry similar to a 3-minute rest in 10 well-trained athletes. Peak force still fell within each set, so staff should expect drop-off from about repetition 4.
paper.methods: Randomized repeated-measures crossover laboratory study. Ten uninjured male athletes who met baseline criteria (eccentric peak force of at least 337 N, asymmetry under 15%, weekly NHE exposure and no lower-limb injury in the prior 6 months) completed 2 sets of 6 repetitions on the NordBord with either a 1-minute or 3-minute interset rest. Peak force, average force, percentage maintenance and interlimb asymmetry were analyzed with 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA.
paper.findings: No main effects or interactions for rest condition were found for any force index or asymmetry (P > .05). Peak force was lower than repetition 1 from repetition 4 onward in set 1 for both limbs, and from repetition 5 onward in set 2 for the dominant limb. Interlimb asymmetry was about 8% to 9% in both conditions and did not change between sets. Percentage maintenance was above 93% across sets.
paper.limitations: Ten participants, one session per condition and a single set pair limit power, so null results do not show the two rest intervals are equivalent; the power analysis used an effect size from a different NHE training study. Inclusion criteria selected injury-free, stronger athletes, so results may not apply to injured or less trained players. Standardized between-condition differences slightly favored the 3-minute rest (small magnitude), and the Key Points mention modest benefits of 3 minutes, but no difference was significant.
paper.practicalImplications: For uninjured athletes already familiar with the NHE, a 1-minute rest between sets did not reduce force or change asymmetry in this study. Because peak force still fell from repetition 4 onward, use fewer repetitions per set or add a brief rest after each repetition. Interpret asymmetry individually, as the authors recommend.
paper.athleteDev: In an eccentric hamstring block for well-trained athletes, a 1-minute interset rest did not cost force. Set structure matters more: plan fewer repetitions or a rest between repetitions, because peak force fell from repetition 4 onward.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport or rehabilitation rest prescription. It tested uninjured athletes only and excluded anyone with a lower-limb injury in the prior 6 months.

records.sourceFile: Divergent performance outcomes following resistance training using repetition maximums or relative intensity.pdf

paper.citation: Carroll KM, Bernards JR, Bazyler CD, Taber CB, Stuart CA, DeWeese BH, et al. Divergent Performance Outcomes Following Resistance Training Using Repetition Maximums or Relative Intensity. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018 (accepted manuscript).
paper.abstract: Fifteen well-trained men completed 10 weeks of resistance training in a repetition maximum (RM, n = 8) or relative intensity by sets and repetitions (RISR, n = 7) group. The RISR group showed moderate between-group effect sizes favoring it for squat and countermovement jump height, and training strain was statistically greater in the RM group, which also showed decreases in early rate of force development.
paper.tldr: Over 10 weeks with similar volume load, relative intensity training with heavy and light days improved jump height and early rate of force development more than repetition maximum training to failure in well-trained men. Both groups gained maximal isometric strength by a similar amount, and with 7 or 8 men per group the findings are preliminary.
paper.methods: Fifteen well-trained men (age 26.9 years) were ranked and paired on baseline allometric isometric peak force, then randomly assigned to repetition maximum zone (RM, n = 8) or relative intensity by sets and repetitions (RISR, n = 7) training for 10 weeks, 3 days per week, plus a common sprint program on two other days. Squat and countermovement jumps (unweighted and 20 kg) and isometric mid-thigh pull peak force and rate of force development were tested at five time points. Mixed-design ANOVAs and Hedges g with 90% confidence intervals (within-group from pre and post values, between-group from change scores) were used.
paper.findings: Volume load displacement did not differ between groups at post hoc testing, but training strain was greater in RM in weeks 3 to 10 (p < 0.05). RISR increased unweighted squat jump height pre to post (p = 0.009) while RM did not, and between-group effects favoured RISR for all jump heights (g = 0.76 to 1.07) and for early RFD (g = 0.89 to 1.25). Isometric peak force rose significantly only in RISR (p < 0.001), although RM showed moderate within-group gains (g = 0.83 to 0.98) and the between-group effect was trivial to small (g = 0.18 to 0.20); RM significantly decreased RFD at 0 to 50 ms (p = 0.018) and 0 to 100 ms (p = 0.014).
paper.limitations: The sample is small (15 men in two groups) with no non-training control and many outcomes; between-group 90% confidence intervals are about plus or minus 0.83, so the CMJ 20 kg jump height (g = 0.76) and all peak force effects include zero. RFD reliability was poor (CV 21 to 24% for 0 to 50 and 0 to 100 ms), and baseline RFD was higher in RM than RISR (for example 5,534 vs 3,646 N/s at 0 to 50 ms), which may contribute to the divergent changes (Inference). The abstract places the taper in weeks 8 to 10, whereas the Methods describe the final two weeks as the taper; this record follows the Methods.
paper.practicalImplications: In well-trained men, varying intensity across the week (heavy and light days, with loads set from set and repetition maxima) gave larger jump and early RFD gains than repeatedly training to failure at similar volume load, which the authors link to lower training strain. Both approaches raised maximal strength, so the choice matters most when jump and rapid force are the goal. Both groups improved after the two-week taper, but there was no no-taper comparison, so the taper's own effect is not isolated.
paper.athleteDev: For jump height and rapid force goals in trained men, the study supports varying loads across the week over repeated sets to failure. For maximal strength alone the two methods gave similar gains. Effects come from 7 to 8 men per group over 10 weeks, so treat the principle as a hypothesis to test with your own athletes.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The sample was well-trained men without injury, and no rehabilitation or return-to-sport outcome was measured, so the study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.
